blocks.x: I was christened by Friday Montgomery Methodist preacher Amos Earl Mordecai White. Amos was all right. The Mordecai was quite complicated because the people in my early life used to call me Mordecai instead of Mordecai as it is properly pronounced. November 6, 1889 was given in the Bible as my date of birth. It was so registered in the county seat, Williamsburg, King Street, South Carolina. My mother's maiden name was Elizabeth Burgess and she was married to Louis White. The date of that I do not know. However, that was also in the Bible which was destroyed. To the Union was born, I'm the first child, five of us. Myself, the oldest, Geneva, the second girl, a girl. The third born was Peter and the baby's next baby was Christina Mary. They're all dead. Pete died in 1944 in Philadelphia. Geneva died while I was still in the Jenkins orphanage in Charleston, South Carolina. My mother was an old county school teacher in one of the rural schools in South Carolina. I don't suppose she got this school from being so capable, but it was just a habit that if a girl attained a certain grade in one of the so-called better schools and Maysville Academy was considered pretty good and nearest to us. Well, after she had attended Maysville, you'd say anyhow, for maybe a couple of terms, years, and the school terms didn't run any more than six months. Well, she came back and applied for a school because she thought she could teach and she did fairly well and lower grades. I used to ride with my mother and the old mule and buggy sometimes. The mule died the next year while they were substituted for a horse and we'd go to the old Heller stable and my father would buy another one to replace the dead mule or horse. I can remember about three or four of them and that's what she went to school. I was always with her. I was placed in the Jenkins orphanage for the first time before I was, I don't remember quite rightly the age bracket, but I know I wasn't nine yet because I wasn't quite nine and my mother died
and that time I had come back home. How old an institution is the Jenkins orphanage?
The Jenkins orphanage was established I think around about 1890, I believe, by the Reverend Jenkins.
You knew him personally then, right? Well, I'm his son-in-law. Oh. I mean you'd known the family right there then before.

No, I didn't know anything about the family before. It happened that he was pastoring a Baptist church called the Siloam Baptist Church in King Street and also the Bethlehem Baptist Church about five miles out from King Street. In those days, the pastor could pastor more than one church if he felt able. If he gave one service here a month to this church and to another, I've known him to have as many as five churches in a circuit. Preach to one in the morning and another in the afternoon. So Mr. Jenkins was pastor of a big church in Charleston, but he accepted the pastor of both these churches on call from offices of the Baptist faith. And so- You were a Baptist then, were you? Well, no, I'm coming to that. I wasn't baptized until I was 14 years of age. At that time, I'm in the Jenkins orphanage in Charleston. My mother is dead now. Yeah. And I'm, I'm over to the orphanage now for a period until I reach manhood, I'm supposing. Well, I was baptized in what they call the Cooper River on this side and the Ashley River on this side of Charleston. Out here is the beach of the Atlantic Ocean. Well, we just weighed down into the beach as far as Mr. Jenkins would allow himself to be carried a little around the waist. I'd say a little above the waist, but not so it would be dangerous. And there's where I was baptized.
Can you remember the music when you were young? Did you play anything or other members of the family?

No members of my family played anything because the fact of it is I was away from my family then. I just considered myself having no family. I knew my sister was at home and I knew Peter was at home with my father in King Street, but the two smaller children, they were dead. And Geneva, she died when I was about 16. She died at around 14. She was kind of chubby and fat and took pneumonia and died. Well, I went back to her funeral. Mr. Jenkins sent me back. I was already a member of the band then also. See, in the printing department, they kept me in the printing department until I, oh I guess I was around about 14 before they even allowed me to touch an instrument. I was a kind of a sickly child. Always coughing, always having had a cold. And they had a doctor who would come there, but he said I had guitar, hay people. So they would avoid putting me in the band, but I wanted to learn music because I could sing. I was a very good singer. So the first season they took me to with the band East. Took me East with the band. You started right on in the carnet? No. Alto Horn. Alto Horn. And the band was taught that season by Eugene Michael. And then, oh, after one season through the East. And these seasons in the East took in everything we would say from, well, Massachusetts straight on down through Pennsylvania, back into Washington, where the Mason and Dixon line ends. Then we'd head for home for school.
And you played on those tours. Where did you play? Concerts or streets?

Concerts. Everything that any band could play. We had an engagement for a month engagement on the boardwalk in Atlantic City, New Jersey, right beside Arthur Pryor's band. And this kid band was really one of the most marvelous boys band in the world. I heard them once. They're only 20 years old. Because they had already been over in England with the Cummings Wild West Circus as a featured attraction in the London Hippodrome. And in 1912, they were, no, this was 1904, one day over there, after they completed an engagement at the St. Louis Fair.
Oh, yeah.

This band also was playing on the Midway at the Buffalo Exposition in 1902. I was not a member of it then. The band under the direction of P.M. Logan, we call him Hotze for a nickname. Professor P.M. Logan, a marvelous musician.
How big is the band? You never mentioned how big it is.

Oh, nothing under 30 pieces. Nothing under 30 pieces at no time. Mr. Jenkins kept it up at that strength for years. In the winter in Florida, when they take the tour down in Florida for the winter season, then it would drill down to say about 20, some odd, maybe 24. Because the bigger boys in the band, the larger and more older boys, they kept them in school. Because he would always stress an education. So the boys who were members of the band, ranging in age from 12 to 16, he put them in the classroom so they could further their education. He'd take the young ones down in Florida. And Mr. P.G. Degas, who is now president of the home now, was always accompanying this band wherever they went. You see, he is the nephew of Mr. Jenkins. And he now, he succeeded to the pastor of the Fourth Baptist Church in Charleston. He's presently there now, if he hasn't passed at this time. Last I heard of it, and that was just about a year or so ago, he was actively heading the institution. This band played inaugural parades for Theodore Roosevelt. I happened to be in that one, 1904. I'm almost 15 now. In 1908, when William Howard Taft was elected president, this band was also in there. That parade. I was in that band. In 1912, for Woodrow Wilson, the Democrats came to power and the Democrats in South Carolina didn't want the Jenkins-Ownage band to appear in this inauguration parade. But the staunch Republicans from upstate saw that the band went just the same. They paid the expenses. Now, there is no other record of any small, uh, kid, Negro band having these honors. Then they went from there to the London stadium. And that was, uh, last year, uh, I served with the band. Because I was already a student in Benedict College in 1900, latter part of 10 and 11. But I, I went with the band East that summer as director of the band. And Mr. Jenkins' son, Edmund, who had won seven consecutive scholarships for clarinet manipulation, violin, piano, and the theory of music, was back, uh, and he took charge of the band. It's quite an honor to have the son of the president directed the band. And he was, he could also play skillfully these, uh, very, very articulate solos on the clarinet, on the pipe organ, he would speak, dance just as accurately as his fingers did almost. And he was called the Black Prodigy of Europe. Incidentally, I might mention here that some things written about music come from people who know nothing about it. In my travels around the country, I had the pleasure of meeting great Negro bands in Tampa, Florida, Key West, the Shackleford family there, Jacksonville, Florida, uh, Willie Lewis, whose son now is a marvelous musician in New York, led the Welcome Cornette band, they called it. There were two bands in Jacksonville, but I'll tell you about that a little later. There were marvelous bands in Savannah and Atlanta. I might mention that, uh, Miller's band in Savannah was well uniformed, well tutored, and played very good. Uh, we had no outstanding bands in South Carolina except the Jenkins orphanage band of Charleston and Tom Pinckney's band of Columbia, South Carolina. While I was a student at Benedict, I played in Tom Pinckney's band. Hardy, who was one of my teachers in my early days in the orphanage, had taken charge of Pinckney's band in Columbia and Hardy put me in the band. So while I was a student at Benedict, I still served in Pinckney's band on occasions. I could name to you several fine bands in America that we had come up against that we had the pleasure of hearing because we were widely traveled, such as Bill Berry's band of St. Louis, Missouri, a band of 50 pieces, whom I heard in concert in New York in 1908. And then Bill went on to Illinois to take charge of the 8th Regiment band, and I heard Bill's band again. So in my travels around the country, I had a chance to hear a little more than the ordinary fellow could hear from staying at home. Even down in Pensacola, Florida down there, they had a wonderful band down there, the Weyer family. Old Man Weyer himself directed the band, and one of the greatest violinists in America, Paul Weyer, is a product of that band. Now the bands down in Pensacola in the lower south never numbered more than 10, hardly more than 15 pieces. They thought they had a heck of a fine band when they had as many as 15 pieces. But no band in the whole United States, nowhere in the world, topped the Jenkins band of Charleston,
South Carolina, and that's the band I came up in. How young were the youngest ones in there usually?

Four years of age. Four years of age. Little Sammy Coates directed the band as a comedy director, however. Yes. Under me, under Hardy, under John Brown, and under Brooks Brockman. Brooks Brockman lived in Los Angeles until about three years ago, and he died. Now, I'm leaving the Jenkins orphanage now. I'm also leaving Benedict College. I didn't stay there, but a term and a half. The president told me the college could very well do without me next year for obvious reasons, some of which I hold as a secret that I know personally of myself. But Dr. Osmond, being the president, warned me that the college could not tolerate certain things. They were not too disgraceful for a young man to admit, but he just said that the college was too religious and couldn't stand this. That was that I would take a drink once in a while.
It's just the truth. How do college students drink now? Well, yes. Same as I don't know.

By me playing out with Pinkney and Johnson, Bill Johnson, the rest of them. Well, they said, come on, take a drink. It won't hurt you, boy. Well, I thought it was right to be obedient to those old men. Well, when I left the office, I ran away with the president's daughter, Dr. Jacksonville, when I got married by Dr. John E. Ford, Bethel Baptist Institutional Church in 1913. You want to cut it off for a minute?
Oh, yes. Okay.

After my marriage to the president's daughter, Roxabel, I took residence in Jacksonville. And my first job was as a printer with the Florida Union Printing Company. Mrs. Saunders owned it. She was a very wealthy Negro woman down there. And this office had been the former office of one of the noted Negro writers, T. Thomas Fortune, whom the world recognizes as one of the greatest editorialists of his day and time. So I worked there for about 10 months. While in Jacksonville, the second biggest band in Jacksonville, numbering about, I suppose, 15 pieces, asked me to become their leader. And that band was the Jacksonville Concert Band. And under Castellana and Dean, realtors in Jacksonville, they established a park out on Davis Street in Jacksonville, Florida, building up a new section out there, residential, for the Negroes of Jacksonville, Florida. The Negro population had begun to grow extensively. Castellana and Dean, biggest realtors in town, cut out this whole plot out there. I suppose, very near, oh, possibly 80 acres or more. And they built a fine band standing around. And every Sunday afternoon, the Jacksonville Concert Band, we gave concerts in this pavilion. For a while, I thought Jacksonville was going to be a really fine place for me. But the old man, whom we called, the old man is Mr. Jenkins, my father-in-law, called me back to Charleston. Everything is reconciled now. So we're on good terms again. And he called me back to Charleston. And he says, take the band to New York, and Edmund will meet you there. This is the second year for Edmund's directorship of the band. Edmund is my brother-in-law, Edmund Jenkins. When Edmund came, he says, I'd rather you take a portion of the band. Now we had about 44 pieces this year, bigger than ever. I want you to take a portion of the band. I want you to take a portion of the band. I want you to take a small unit of it and play this Uncle Tom's Cabin production.
At the old Columbia Theater. I think it was on 47th Street, I don't remember where. Oh, right on Broadway. Yeah. Yeah, I remember.

Yeah, so I took a portion of the band down there, 11 fellas, and we played this Uncle Tom's Cabin production there. Well, then I began to trek around the country with circuses and minstrel shows and so forth. My first minstrel show was the Franks New York Minstrels out of Birmingham, Alabama. In 1914, I went off on a tour with that minstrel show. But the show busted up after coming out through Virginia into Tennessee. They busted up in a little town called Pulaski, Tennessee. And then I taught a little band in Pulaski during the winter there in Dixon, Pulaski, and Columbia, each. These three little towns. They weren't no more than about nine miles apart from different directors around. But when the warm months, months began to get warm, I looked for another show. And you could always find lucrative work in the Billboard, which was a show publication. Oh, yeah. So I joined up with the Alabama Minstrels. And for a season on the Alabama Minstrels, I was with Jeff Smith under his direction. One of the greatest musicians I have ever known in my life. Fine cornet soloists, the best I've ever listened to. And a wonderful interpreter of the concert scores. Something that I didn't actually get a whole lot of, that is the larger compositions, in the orphanage. The point is they didn't play heavy overtures, but we played modern
songs and marches. How big a band did those minstrel shows have?
Well, Jeff at that time had 24 pieces. 24 pieces.
Was it like an orchestra or brass band? Out of that we had always a ten piece orchestra

to play the show in the pit. We had violinists, piccolo players, bass viol players, all of the instruments that go along. We had five clarinets in this band, and a fine piccolo player, Jared. And later on we got Clarence Owens, who now directs the 8th Regiment Band in Chicago. 8th Illinois Regiment. Ward officer Clarence Owens. The next season Jeff quit, and the manager of the of the Minstrel show asked me would I take the band over. I said, Charles E. Boeing. And I did. But I didn't complete the season, because another show offered me more money, and that was the Harveys Minstrel. Their home was in St. Paul, Minnesota, but they call it the New Orleans Minstrels. Never had seen New Orleans. The closest they ever got to New Orleans was when the winter season closed in Homer, Louisiana. And the two fine Pullman cars put up on the siding there. And while in Homer for a few days, I chanced to meet Arthur and Albert Verrett in 1917. Was Bunk Johnson around in that time? Bunk Johnson was around in those days. Bunk Johnson was definitely around. Well, I played a winter down there with the Verrett boys, Arthur and Albert Verrett. They had a seven piece orchestra down there. Albert played the violin and conducted the orchestra. And he was an excellent reader. That's Albert. But he was tripled. And Arthur played the saxophone and clarinet. I played trumpet. Young, Billy Young. I forgot what his father's name was. But anyhow, everybody called him Professor Young. He was not in Homer at that time, but Young was our trombone player. And Arthur and Albert had a sister who played the piano very well, but all halls did not have pianos in them. So we had a good bass player. And his name was Harrison. And we had a drummer. We called him Neegi. And that's all I ever knew from my whole state out there. He was a drummer, a very good drummer. And we had a banjo player. He was a barber down there. And if I'm not mistaken, I think his name was Barnes, I believe.
Planet player?

No, no. Banjo player. Banjo player. There were two Barnes's down there. But I think this fella's name was Barnes too. Isaac Barnes, I believe. That was in the Barnes that Louis went to. I believe. And during this winter down there while I was there, they advertised that this fella, another Barnes there who all tried to have a man around, he sent to New Orleans and brought Louis up there to play with him. I never got a chance to meet Louis personally, but I heard him the night of the affair. We had an engagement also. We used to play out both ends of the bar, up north end and up the south end. Always the Cajuns, wherever the Verrett boys were playing, where they flocked just like a bunch of blackbirds to a rice field. They were crowded. We were never without an audience of hundreds for any of our engagements. That's how good the Verrett brothers orchestra was at home. Well, I had begun to absorb a little bit of the New Orleans style of playing, because the fellas would tell me, listen to so-and-so, listen to so-and-so, listen to this fella, listen to that one and so forth. And the solid beat and the legato tone, the sort of a languid tone, you know. I had begun to develop a part of it from a fella named, one-armed fella named Joe Porter. Joe Porter.
Was the New Orleans style you felt different? Was that the New Orleans influence?

Yes, they had the New Orleans style down there too. Those boys definitely had, they had the stomp and the beat and everything on the New Orleans style. Well, I began to like it so well, till after my winter closed in 1917, I went back down there. Tell me this, say in the east,
around Florida and North Carolina, even further north, had you come across any style like that? Well- Is there a difference in the Louisiana style, say, and the other east?

Very, very different. Very different. There was no style, nowhere in the United States similar to the style of the playing of the fellas around in lower Louisiana and especially New Orleans. They had variations on the theme, whatever the number was. They had such variations on such wide variety of variations, until it would astound you. Yeah, it did me when I first started. Yes, that's just the truth. Now in places like Jacksonville, we had wonderful musicians around Jacksonville, like Tony Jackson and Connie Michael and fellas like that, Willie Lewis, whom I mentioned a while ago. They played, but they played just as near correct as they could. Stuck right to the note. Yeah. Well, you take the Johnson brothers, Dr. Weldon Johnson and James Roseman Johnson, that's their home. Then I had a fellow named Shermie playing cornet with me out of the Edward Waters College there in the Jacksonville concert band. He used to play in one of the ragtime bands around Jacksonville and then Love Lee. And while I'm on the Jacksonville subject here, a wonderful band. Jacksonville had a wonderful band, but it was never stationed in Jacksonville as a Jacksonville's own. Because this fine musician, Eugene Michael, having resigned his position at Tuskegee Institute, he was a sort of a musician on tour always. And he would always come and bring his fine band of musicians off some concert tour to Jacksonville. And he always carried 25 pieces. Michael was a fine director, fine pianist, fine violinist, and a beautiful cornetist. Not nothing exciting, but just a strictly business cornet player. Fine.
Anytime you want to answer the phone or anything, we can always stop.
Yeah. Yeah, it does.
Is that for you? Okay, it's all in the end.

All right. Then I, for my season, 1918, I began that season with the Cole Brothers Circus under the directorship of J.C. Myers, the husband of Lizzie Myers. Contrary to what another publisher said about he being the father, that's not true. That was her husband. George, yeah. And, uh, that's right. And J.C. Myers' minstrel shows on the Cole Brothers Circus was a unit similar to the Georgia Smart Set, the Alabama minstrels, and the Virginia minstrels. The man owned all of those shows. In fact, the Cole Brothers Circus was the second, was the largest circus, but they had another one called the Spock Circus that they had bought also.
I think I've seen the Cole Brothers Circus from the last year.

Then the Jones Brothers and Wilson Circus of 30 Cars. Well, Elmer Jones and Augusta Jones was the owner of all those shows. Three circuses and three outstanding minstrel attractions. And they were fine shows. There was no disgrace to belong to one of them. They had big bands. The band on the Virginia minstrels was conducted by, uh, Frank Moreland, the father of Mantaan. And Frank Moreland was a wonderful bandmaster. The band on the Virginia minstrels was conducted by Ayers first. And, uh, uh, then later on by, um, what's his name? He lived in Greenville, South Carolina. Max something. But anyhow, it was another wonderful band. And the band on the Alabama minstrels was conducted in variance by four different men. First, Jeff Smith. Next, me. Next, Charlie Lewis. Next, Edward Howard. And he lives in Washington, D.C. now.
And? Tell us a little bit about the Georgia Smart Set, because this is a very close friend. I had Buck Johnson, who I remember.
Yeah, that's right. Thanks for them.
That's right. He never got to tell me anything about it. That's right.

So, you can tell me a little bit about it. Well, Buck, Buck served the season on the, on the Georgia Smart Set, uh, under Frank Moreland. Uh, and Buck was a featured man in the way he played. And Buck was a very fine jazz man. And he had a distinct way of, of playing the special numbers that Frank would allocate him to play at the Noonday concert was, was a, a send off to the band. The same as after, after I had spent a season in New Orleans down there, and I come to this later, because this is 1924 when I took a little squirt with the Alabama minstrels just for a few months. They featured me in the New Orleans style. And Eddie Howard. And I had to play a few numbers out there for Mr. Bowman, who was the manager of the show. He'd come out to hear these numbers, like the St. Louis Blues and the High Society. They liked to hear me play those numbers. And I was featured with them. But I also had to play an intricate solo at times too. I had also, I sometimes was called upon to play a decent solo, like a triple-tongue poker. And for those triple-tongue pokers, I played short and sweet, three-style poker, and, and my old Kentucky home. I played my old Kentucky home in my own variations, three variations. A six-eight movement, a two-four movement, and then the last movement, two-four, but the last eight or twelve or sixteen measures in triple-tongue. And then the last one, I was a kid. Now, I, uh, when I came out of the Army, well, I haven't told you about the Army in the first place. In Sedalia, Missouri, I'm with the Cole Brothers Circus, and the United States commissioners, investigators, came in the tent right after a horse had, I mean, the lions had almost ate of a horse in the surface. Well, Lizzie was on the surface then, and she had these beautiful pigeons on her shoulder that would light around as she paraded around in the pageant. Now, we have-
She rode the horse too, or no?

Oh, yes. She rode the horse bareback, I think, with just the flannel over to keep her dress clean, but she was always beautifully gowned. And these pigeons made a perfect pitch out of her, because she was a beautiful woman in those days. And Mr. Jones and the circus would so acclaim her. And with these pigeons, the white pigeons, you know, with a little streak in the wings, lighting on her shoulder, she made a picture, a picture that you couldn't resist looking at. And these were flashing on the billboards, see? So they just flocked to the circus. Now, we're playing the State Fair with Behuma Crill's band.
I heard Ben, Mr. Taukman.

Uh-huh. And the Cole Brothers Circus was playing there as a special attraction, and Miles has 15 pieces in his band. But I'm Miles' bandmaster, because Miles liked to play the drums to keep the tempo out. So I have to take over for Miles. That's Joel Morris playing there also. And the little Jap Loveless, he's there. And then is when I had to really cut it, because the bulk of the work was on me, playing all of these gallops and fast marches and sailing from one number to another, you know. You're playing the big show now. They had no white band on the show. So then we'd split up and take six pieces and go over and play the side show. They called it the jig show. And the other nine pieces would play in the State Fair and play the circus. I was always with this nine pieces because the bulk of the work was in the Big Ten. Well, when the commissioners came through and I didn't have my registration card with me, why they just said, well, the card was in the, my registration card was in the privileged car now. But they wouldn't allow you to get it because the order was.
All right.

Yeah, and when they asked for the card, there were about five of us in there who were supposed to be fellows of war age. And I didn't have my card in my pocket. The fact of it is I had gone to the circus that day in my shirt sleeve because we put on our band coats in the tent, under the tent. And well, where's your card? And they got right hostile with me, you know. They grabbed me. I said, it's down the privilege card. No, you won't go get anything, they said. We're going to take you on in. You were instructed to have that card on you. So they took me straight on to the jail. And then I got busy. Miles went and got my card, brought it to me. But by that time, the commissioners have all gone. So now I got to spend this night in there. And this is on a Saturday afternoon. Now this is Sunday and Miles is off. So Miles came to the jail and brought me my week's salary and some more money. I think he all totally gave me about $40. And he brought some clothes to me. And I said, well, I don't need any clothes because I'm going on to the Army. I know it. He brought my card to me. Well, when the commissioners came to sit in Sunday afternoon and Sheriff Dawes was the sheriff there in Nevada, Missouri. You see, they didn't take me up in Sedalia. Well, they took me where the regular United States commissioner's office was, and that was in Nevada, Missouri. They had different points for these places and states. And regardless of the fact that Sedalia was a much bigger city than Nevada, still they took me to Nevada. After I approved registration and everything, they were no longer hostile. They had a commissioner. Three commissioners came in on a Sunday afternoon on request of Sheriff Dawes. Sheriff Dawes said, well, I don't see what they want to keep you in here for. You approved registration. You got your card and everything. He says, I'm going to call them up down there. They're still in. So they made a special trip back there to jail and they sat in and said, well, what do you want to do? You didn't have that card on you. I said, I want to go to the service. I said, the fact of it is I had written Mr. Michael, Eugene Michael, my former teacher. I had written James Reese Europe because a lot of boys out of the Jenkins office was in his band, just a whole lot. In fact, the boy who killed James Reese Europe was a student of mine, Herbert Wright, but only, yeah, but I was just about a few months older than Herbert. Well, they sent me on to camp. I rode all that evening. No sheriff went there or anything. And all that night, I sidetracked on the road in a little town in Kansas, some place way down the border there, going to Camp Funston. That was in Kansas? No, this was in Missouri where I was in jail. But now they're sending me to camp. On this long trek to Camp Funston, you got to cut around through the corner of Missouri, cut around through the corner of Oklahoma and to Kansas, and then go up to Camp Funston, you see. You see, that's the way they— I don't remember where it was. It's time. Camp Funston is way up in the corner of Kansas. Where is it now?
I can't picture it. It's in Kansas, though.
Yeah, it's in Kansas, but it's not in central Kansas. You're almost over to the mountainous side. You're almost around to the Colorado corner.
Colorado or South Dakota. New Mexico.

New Mexico. But anyhow, it's cold up around there. Well, I finally reached Camp Funston on one of these old slow trains, but it looked like they didn't care how you traveled in those days, you see, army movements. I reached Camp Funston along about two o'clock in the afternoon. Maybe it might have been a little earlier than that, but anyhow, when I got to the gate, I had my trumpet with me and I had a little bag. I had an extra pair of shoes there, an extra pair of pants. I don't know why I carried them along. I knew I was going to need them. I didn't think so anyhow. But anyhow, just to be ready for an occasion. And the sergeant at the gate said to me, where is the sheriff who brought you here? I told him, I said, no sheriff brought me here. Yes, you did. Where is the man who brought you here? And he kept on asking me. I said, no man brought me here. And what I said, and I said kind of forcibly, I said, I came unguarded here. He slapped me. And I didn't say nothing. I just took the little slap and I kind of halfway grinned. But brother, all the hell and fury had gotten into me then. If I must go to war, don't beat me up before I get in there. All right.
So he pushed me down through the gate. Go on in there.

I went in the gate and I went straight on up the step. Now, my plan of action is already in me. I know what to do because I've had a little military training in the schools. They taught us military training in James. They also carried some drill tactics in Benedict and all the colleges down there. They didn't have no regular ROTC.
Yeah.

Go ahead. But the order of the day had to be obeyed in the colleges and in the schools all through the South. When I got in, I asked for the officer in charge. So they referred me to a major over there who afterwards became one of my majors, Major Blaine. And I saluted, came to attention and I had no training but I knew this had to be done. And I said, sir, I'm Private Amos Mordecai White reporting from Nevada, Missouri. I was arrested two days ago for not having my card on me. I had the card and I came here unguarded. Sheriff Dawes granted me that privilege because he saw I wanted to get in the Army. I have no near relatives to which my paper could be sent that I might have received them. So I, the best thing for me to do is to have my mail sent en route with the circus because I'm on the Cole Brothers' circus this season. And I said, as I came in the gate, the officer, the non-commissioned officer at the gate slapped me and kicked me and beat me up at the gate. I put it all in straw. He said, said to his orderly, go to the gate and bring that sergeant at the gate here. I brought this tall sergeant at Gawkes Camp from Georgia. And he says, that's Sergeant Major. He says, come here. He called him over to me. He snatched the chevron off first. I'm about, Sergeant Major, what's that? He says, for kicking and hitting this man at the gate. While he's trying to give you an explanation for coming into the service. Take him to the guardhouse and put him in there and lock him up and throw the key away until I tell you when to pick it up. And I laughed. And I said, ha, ha, ha. And when I laughed, the Major told me, shut up. And stand at attention. Yes, sir. I don't even know for my mouth. Well, he sent me into the D-cootie. I had no more than got my uniform on and delivered to me. I didn't even have them strapped to the legs around me or anything. When they called me, said, fall out! Fall out! Line out! Any of you fellas here? Of you crutes? This is old Sergeant Clark talking now. Know how to type right? I said, me! Step us two paces forward. Sent me to the office. I got there, start picking at the type right. I could type correctly, but I couldn't type faster. I had no keyboard back. Printing, you see the case on the printing case is almost similar. But any man who can print correctly and observe punctuations and capitalizations, you can type you don't let them better than one of these half-handed, ill-tuted supposed secretaries. Well, I typed out a letter for him. Typed it out quicker than anybody in there, too. My nervous self. That's good, sir.
All right.

They dismiss me out. Go to your barracks. I'll go over to the YMCA. Fall out again in a half an hour. Next time, fall in! I'm out again. How many of you men in here have had any office work experience? Me. I had experience in everything. But the last call they issued around about six o'clock. You know, the sun's way up. How many musicians are in this rank?
Me.

Me. Me. Nine fellas down the line held their hands up. Another rank over here. The sergeant was asking the same thing over there. About eleven from over there held their hands up. All right. All you men report to the YMC. So, into the YMC, well, about twenty-four of us. And when we assembled in the YMC, there was a lieutenant there, just out of the Chautauqua band. Canadian Kilties. You remember that band, the Canadian Kilties?
I remember that band.

Oh, they were fine. We dated them down in Clovis, New Mexico one time. But that's either here or there. Anyhow, this fellow was already in his first lieutenant's uniform. And they had sent him to take charge of the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band. He held a rehearsal with we twenty-four fellas. And he says, I'll have another rehearsal tonight at nine o'clock. This is long, about six o'clock. That night at nine o'clock, we were all assembled in there again. He says, I'm going to have an elimination contest in here. He says, because I have gotten new orders. I'm going to be a line officer and there is promotion for me. And there is a chance for one of you men in this outfit to become the band leader of this regiment now being formed. He says, the 806th and the 805th Pioneer Infantry have already been formed. And they are now in regimented and in structures ready for sailing. Now this is my second day in camp. He says, one of you men in here are going to take charge of the 816th van temporarily. Because I'm going to recommend, so recommend it to the Colonel in charge here. And the Colonel of the 816th is going to be Colonel L.A. I. Chapman. Colonel Chapman he just called. I was learning his initials. And your Lieutenant Colonel is going to be Lieutenant Colonel Pottle. And Lieutenant Colonel Pottle will be over here in a few minutes because he wants this unit to do guard mount tomorrow. Okay, finally. So the first thing he put up is, Espanol Waltz. You don't want me to say that I guess. I remember that. Alright, so he put up that and he says, now I'm going to start conducting. And I'm not, I'm going to disregard all of your mistakes. But the man, when I am through conducting, if the man I find playing, as long as I'm conducting, and finishes up according to the measure or the strain where I am, that man will be considered the bandmaster here. So he went all the way down until he came to the, I think the C section. You know, Waltz is written there. C is the one. And where you have to, it's a Dalsignal sign there. And then you must go back up to the very first strain and then, we lay there at the end of that strain down to D. Well, he, when he, when he, when he observed his, that signal sound, or the kapo, and got back down that strain, he cut off. And you see, the thing of it is that I stress with my fellows always, you keep your eye glued here, but let the shadow of that baton be seen by you also. If you don't observe the shadow of this baton, you're not playing according to the direction. Yeah, I know you have to read the music down there, certainly, but the shadow of this baton will also be seen by you. Even if you read that music, you can keep one eye glued down here for your next measure, and you can still see the shadow of that baton. Of course, there's a little, little flair in there. I might as well tell you about it. I had played the waltz before. Wasn't anybody playing with me.
He said, what's your name?

I said, Amos, Mordecai, White. Step out. Hey, fellas, here's your bandmaster. Now, I'll be a line officer, and good luck to you. You play a wonderful trumpet. I was playing then a JW York and son trumpet, and he had an EA Couturier trumpet. And that made me have a love for the Couturier horn, and I bought the 10,000th instrument. No, 1,000th some odd. 1076. My boy's got, my grandson has the trumpet out there now. 1076, designed by EA Couturier and Sons. La Porte, Indiana. After he came to America to demonstrate for the Holden Company. Well, then that began my tenure with the 816 Piney Infantry. In the next five days, we were on the train, making Liberty long drives in cities. The first city out of, out of, uh, Camp Funston was Kansas City, Missouri. And Kansas City, Missouri to St. Louis. St. Louis to Indianapolis. St. Louis to Columbus, Ohio. Columbus, Ohio to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And strangely, we jumped all the way back cross country, some roundabout way to Cleveland. And, uh, went up to, uh, Omaha, Nebraska, uh, to St. Paul. And, uh, doubled back in there, about three days riding, making Liberty long drives in various cities. And the band wasn't so well rehearsed, but they had a chance. We, they gave us a whole, uh, uh, boxcar. And we'd sit in this boxcar, and they'd serve us meals in there at these various points. And the Red Cross, and everybody else was giving us fine food on the route. And put birth in there for us. And then those travelers, the four days, the band became a very well-constructed unit. But when I got to, uh, uh, Camp Upton, Long Island, where I, they had recruited about seventeen more men out of Fort Riley. And they had sent them to me also. They came out with William Triggs. A fellow named William Triggs, who after they became my first sighted in the band. And then I got, I think I got about, uh, four fellas right out of Camp Upton. And the band's strength then was brought up to fully 47. 47. And we stayed in the water out there a day and a night, or maybe a little longer. I don't remember which one, I stayed seasick from the time I got on the boat until I got across almost.
Oh. You guys, Maurice Durand was in that.
Yeah, yeah, he was right there. And Maurice Durand was a feature in that he could play the, the hook and car blues. And he, we had another, what that mule, piece in the other mule calls in it.
I don't remember, I remember some sort of race track numbers or what I say about that.
Well anyhow, he used to do the feature on that one.
Oh, there's Livery Stable. Livery Stable blues.

That was his, that was his big feature. And I would always call him out for that number. Yeah, he featured that and played it good too. And he had such strong, devilish lips. He didn't have the proper tone like Hatton had, Frank Hatton or Carl Travis or Robert Walker or Willie Triggs. See, I had ace trumpet players, good ones. They were very, very good. Willie Triggs was the outstanding trumpet player on the Georgia Misses before he came to the Army. And Robert D. Walker was a featured player in Handy's band. And Carl Travis was in Bill Berry's band in St. Louis. And they were good, very good. I didn't have any trouble with my trumpet players. And I had four fine melaphone players. And I had saxophones galore, plenty of them. I didn't have saxophones enough for them. Eddie T. Moore out of Tuskegee band was a bassoon and oboe player. They didn't give us any bassoon. So he played baritone sax. And he did justice to it always. The band was well, well qualified. And while in France, why, I told you that we had to play for this 33rd Division passing in review, they had no band capable of passing them in review and observing all the signals of an officer. Well, I had a fellow named George Wells. He'd been in the 10th Cavalry. He's tall, very handsome youngster. And he knew all the signals for a band, for a observance of an officer in review passing. And he carried them out to the left. While I only stood to the left of my band, you know. And we stayed in this review passing for, oh, from 9 o'clock in the morning until after 4 in the afternoon. Then we hiked on down to Southampton. And all of this hiking, we played limited long drives in England also, in cities as we passed through them. And we crossed the channel at midnight there for La Havre, France. We got over in La Havre while we were underground trains, straight on up through the middle of Paris. And when we got right near this big city of Lille, which was a railroad center in France, then we came up, surfaced up. It was well guarded around there. They were all watching for the Germans to attack them any time. And right out from Lille, we had to go underground again and dugouts and so forth. So we just went on a crawling train on what they call now the 40 and 8. That boxcar that holds 12 hogs. No. Yeah, 12 hogs, 8 horses, or 24 men. Chavez hombres, you see. I don't, I've forgotten what they call a horse, but anyhow, it's a swine name in French. I forgot my French. I could remember it easily by referring to some of the old records.
Cochon or something like that.
Yeah. Cochon. Cochon. Yeah. Yeah. 8 horses, 12 cochons. 12 hogs. Oh yeah, 24 hombres.
Yeah.

Well, then began the history of the 816th Band. Well, the history of the 816th Band measures up very creditably. In that while we were stationed in Verdun, every afternoon except Saturday and Sundays, we had to play a concert in Chevert Square in Verdun. Aside from other planes that we did around in various camps, I serenaded Harry Truman over there, his regiment, Captain Harry Truman. But I didn't know it was Captain Harry Truman. I knew it was Captain Harry Truman there, but I heard no more about him until he became senator, United States Senator. When we arrived out of the camp with the two truckloads of instruments and the two truckload load of band and jumped out while he was sitting at the piano playing.
Oh, you remember that?

Yeah, sure. Yeah, sure. And so, when we walked in, I said, I'm reporting from the 816th Finan Enfrager on the orders of Colonel Chaplin to come up here and serenade you. He said, hell, we don't need any serenading up here. I'll do it to serenade. He said, go on back there and get you something to eat and you can go on back to camp. Oh, he's a wonderful guy, you know. That's why I love him until today. He was so forthright. Great man. But, back to the regiment of band activities. Now, when they started building this big cemetery out from Burden in a little town called Montfaucon, Romaine, a little town just beyond Montfaucon where the cemetery presently is situated now, I suppose, if it hasn't been demolished. Why, we were stationed up there for, from March the 8th until June the 8th. And then the construction of this cemetery, now, my band was never called to do any work in the work. All we were required to do was to entertain the boys and we were given our company street and company barracks. We put up our big tents and I had the tent at the head of the barracks and here was the Colonel's quarters down here. And, I dined with the, in the Colonel's quarters, not with the Colonel and the staff, but I dined in his quarters. The better, higher non-commissioned officers all dined over there. A little better service too, strange to say. I don't want to be different from the men, create a little jealousy. But, that, that was the way it was handled. I had to obey the orders of the, of the other higher non-coms. Of course, I was the highest non-com in my regiment. I was acting warrant officer. I was never commissioned, however. But, I drew the salary of a warrant officer and I had the power of a warrant officer. Mine was only as an assistant bandmaster. That's the rank, permanent rank. That's the discharge rank too. Because, no commission was ever signed and you don't go over the commissions. But, I was the bandmaster, the recognized bandmaster. And, I had no other bandmaster over me at any time. I had no other officer over me. All my conducting of my band over there was done with, with me alone as the sole arbiter of anything. I serenaded, uh, General John J. Pershing four times. But, the ground breaking for the cemetery building, he was there. My band sat right under the stand. My band did the salutation number for his entry. At the closing, my band played the Stars and Stripes and the French national anthem. The French national anthem first and the Stars and Stripes last in France. At the conclusion of this cemetery, General Pershing was up there again to set the flag up and acclaim the cemetery, the largest in the world. And, this was a big day. On the 8th day of June, 1919. And, again, my band was a host band to General John J. Pershing. Now then, right after that, we were supposed to go down and take his band's place at Shawmont. But, orders from General Smedley D. Butler, uh, at La Havre, changed the orders. He set the order that the 816 Pioneer Infantry would sail in August for the United States. When we got to La Havre, France, my General Smedley D. Butler proclaimed, this band is now the Army Camps Band and you are disassociated with the 816 Pioneer Infantry. That's when Maurice left me and went to the hospital. Well, we, each day, our only requirements, whether we play a concert in the Y at a little afternoon or before noon, sometimes early in the morning. I got all my orders from him, typewritten orders. Your band will entrain today and play for so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so. Such, uh, dignitaries would be arriving, you know, and the soldiers were in training for home. Uh, then, you would proceed down to the docks today at 2.30, and there you will stand guard and play for the sailing of troops home until 8 o'clock tonight. So, you see, my band had unusual privileges down in La Havre. And, and during the loading of a ship here and the sailing of that ship, and another ship would come in and another bunch of soldiers would come in, they had lead. So, they'd run all around the town. And some of them came back with saxoconiac. We had a very good time there. And my boys was very obedient to every wish of mine. While they were beating up other bandmasters over there, and they threw one overboard coming back. Really? They threw one bandmaster over the ship. And then it was, they, they'd whip up a bandmaster in a minute. Especially if you were a non-commissioned bandmaster, you didn't have any voice. They'd whip up an officer for that matter. They were mad to come home. But my band was just as jubilant over coming home. But yet, well, I had to be somewhat conciliatory with them, you know. Well, you'll be home pretty soon. I wonder if they're going to keep us in the army. Some of them would say, I said, oh no, you'll be mustered out as soon as you get over there. Little did I think that that would be done, but that was my word to them. And sure enough, well, we came back safe. We gave a concert on the ship, coming back every day. We got back in 11 days. But we stayed in La Hava down there for a solid 24 days. And, yeah, and we had a wonderful time there in La Hava. After I got my discharge in Louisville, Kentucky, I headed down to New Orleans. Because I knew JC Miles had passed. And I knew Lizzie down there. And I didn't know anybody else much in America where I wanted to go. And so I went down to New Orleans. It wasn't with the idea that I'd go down to wait anybody. That's completely out of the question. But I went down there because I had a friend down there. And I still consider her one of my greatest friends. But she is so, she's such a devout Catholic and a good Christian person. That's right. And it would be shameless for me to say anything different about her. She befriended me so many times. And even while she was out here. And I got some letters back there. Letters as late as 1957, the last letters. Just the early part of last year when she had been to the Tin Angel over there. But she had gone back home to take care of her home. And, uh...
By the way, Lizzie's coming out here to Monterey and I guess next month. Is she?

I'll be down there. I'll be down there. Now, during my stay down in New Orleans, I got married after I... Came back here. I got married in 1920 to a girl named Hazel Robinson in New Orleans. She was a beautician and a very fine person. And I happened to be living right in the same block on Murray Street. Where her mother had a cafe at the corner. And Hazel and I struck up a friendship because I was doing her printing. And I got mustered out of the service. I, instead of looking for music to play or trooping any longer, I went to work in my trade. But I had almost forgotten that I was a printer.
How many of you are in New Orleans? Yeah.

So I walked up Rampart Street one day after I bought my first new suit after getting out of the service. Born Art Clothing Store. You know where Born Art is there. And, uh... And I got on the other side of just a little up from Poitras. And, uh, I saw this printing office. Allies Printery. And the door was open. A young lady was sitting behind the desk. Her name was Mary Dupree. And, uh, an elderly, stoop-shouldered white man was at the desk and he was covering some papers. And so I just forced myself. I walked in and I said, how do you do, sir? And so, Miss Dupree, she got up and said, can I help you? And I told her, I said, well, I'm a printer and I'm kind of looking around to find a job someplace. She said, Mr. Garnier, Mr. Garnier, here's a printer. And Mary said to me, we've been looking for a printer. I saw the office and it was a well-equipped office. There were three job presses. There was a linotype machine sitting here. There was a cylinder back there. There were stones. There was planning machines. There were stones over here. And chasers and everything. And such a big, fine printing office. I looked and I said, you don't have any printer here? Mr. Garnier said, no, I don't have no printer here, no. You know, he talked like Creole. And he was a Creole. Garnier. He said, I look for a printer, but I want a good printer, he said. I said, well, I'm a good printer. How long have you been working at the trade? I said, I haven't been working at the trade. I said, I'm just out of the army. He said, if you're just out of the army, you don't print it. You don't print it. I said, well, you try me. He said, I got three jobs here to put up. He sold me three throwaways. And he says, I want these jobs out. And I suppose this was long about 11 o'clock in the day.
I said, the case here, you have to find a type.

I said, I'll find them. So I dropped around and then I scanned out faces here. And the cases were laid out in series, you see. I set up one six by nine in all series. I set up another six by nine in all series. I set up another in all series. And he had plenty of type. Find this equipped job shop in New Orleans, boy. Not to be busy. I throw these three handbills on one after one. Thousands of each of them. And when he came back around four o'clock, all the jobs were stacked up there and ready for me. He looked at me. Where you learn your printing? I said, in Jenkins Orpens in Charleston, South Carolina. My God. I said, man, you're a good printer.
You're a fast printer.
He said, how much do you think that would? I said, well, about, say, six dollars a thousand. Oh, no, no, no, no.
I get a dollar half a thousand from him. I said, oh, you can't work with me. You got a dollar half a thousand.

You got a dollar half a thousand. You can't get. I said, the paper costs more than that. How much you want to work for me? He said, I said, $25 a week. You make the price on the job and everything? I said, I'll price all the jobs. You give the people good work? I said, I'll give them good work. Where you learn estimating at? I said, I've had charge of the job department of the Charleston Metro ever since I was a boy. I said, I can price my job, and I can price the stock, and I'll give you a profit. I said, but if I make it, you must pay me. He said, you talk mighty big. You must know what you do. I said, well, I'm a big man. Little shrimp, you know. He looked at me, cut my arm, said, good boy, you go to work. He said, you price the job. Mary, he said, you take his orders. So Mary was a very beaten young girl. She come up from St. Martinsville, Paris, down there, fine-looking, beautiful girl. And we had no relationship other than a business way, but she was all business. She had graduated from that college down there under Professor somebody, Turo or somebody. They had a business college down there in the Pithian Temple that taught these girls typing and business acumen. And she was very good. She kept an account of everybody. I said, all six by nines are $6.50 a thousand. All calling cards are $2.25 per hundred, $4.50, $5.00, $7.50 a thousand. I set the price. She said, you gonna be in competition with the boy up Dryad Street? And I said, okay, I wanna do better work than they're doing. And I did. And I started printing the contracts with the musicians. The first musician I met was Buddy Petit. And Buddy Petit came in there and he stopped, I want some cards printed. He said, can I get them today? I said, sure you can get them today. My name is Buddy Petit, he said. I said, my name is Amos Mordecai White. So you a printer here? I said, yeah. I printed some bills around here where it says Buddy Petit's band, so you a musician, aren't you? Yeah, I'm a musician. I'm a trumpet player. I'm here, I'm a trumpet player. So he had his claridad player with him. What did you call that boy? Zeb. Zeb. Zeb was with him. And he's having him start bragging on themselves. I said, good, good. I said, that's fine. And then I was glad to meet him. I said, but let me get your card in there. And if they talk right on, I'm putting the card up for him. So while he was waiting there, I printed the cards for him. One hundred. Oh, and Buddy took a light to me. You play music too? I said, yes, I'm just out of the army. I'm a former bandmaster in the army. Yeah? So he started telling the boys all around town. So they started coming in there to get their printing done. You see? Next fellow I met down there was Arnold Matoia. He dropped in one day along with Lizzie. And Lizzie said, I'm going to bring him up on the Temple roof garden tonight. So I don't have any horn. They took my horn from me. Took my own horn from me in the army. I had a whole, I mean I had a york trumpet that I carried in the service with me. And they took that too. And of course the army band instruments had all USA stamped on them, you see. And mine wasn't stamped, but it happened so now. They wouldn't have taken mine. But mine was in the material. Army band material. All that we had stacked up and allowed to put away. And mine was all that. And I intend to pick up my cornet and bring it along with me. And to my surprise the things that we did.
The
Buddy,
Lizzie Miles taking you to the
Well, when Lizzie and Matoya, Arnold Matoya came in the shop, Matoya started with the

Oh no, you wouldn't want to travel around anymore now. You wouldn't want to travel all over the country. No, I wouldn't want to. Although you certainly look young and active, you could do it if you'd like to do it too.

I'd like for you to go downstairs and see my wonderful library down there. I think really I've got a library of music down there that's creditable. We do want to go down. See how much I've got anyhow. You couldn't appraise it. I can't appraise it myself.

Oh no, you can't figure that. No. I'm wondering, just about you here, if there's anything else, there's one thing we might, any other corrections to that other story that was published about you. For instance, the one thing, you were never a night watchman. No, I never was a night watchman.
Any other errors that you wanted to make a note of? Yeah, and I never was in any jail for any length of time for any conviction to come upon me.
Yeah, yeah.
I never had a committed an offense except not having my card with me. Card with me, yeah. And that's been claimed by the War Department and the United States Army even while I was in the service.
Certainly you wouldn't have been in the service.

And now I hold a, not only a citation of honorable merit of the service, but a citation letter from my colonel. And the letter reads, a very valuable soldier to the United States Army. My best wishes go with you and I hope you will make a career of the service. And I could have made a career of the service because at that time there were four regular organized Negro regiments and I could have gone to any one of the bands at the request of their then band masters. And as early as the breakout of World War II, I was asked to come back down to Fort Huachuca and join the band which now is being conducted by, by Crawford in Germany. Crawford was the first chair trumpet player and Mr. Hammond was the band master. And Mr. Hammond passed in Phoenix, Arizona here last year, this year. And Mr. Hammond asked me to come back to the band and he was one of the most discriminating band masters the United States Army ever had.

I don't want to keep you more in a minute. I was trying to ask, when I was young, the only Negro band I ever heard of is the James Reese Europe band in the Army. Did yours compare? Was it anything bigger or special more than say the band like you had? Well, I don't try to be modest and say mine wasn't as good as this. I mean, actually in your opinion. That's right. Was your band in a class better or good?

I'll give you my, I'll give you my own personal appraisal of his band. His band had such entertainers in it as Bill Robinson, Noble Sissel, a few other dancers, a few other singers, a few other people whom in my estimation I considered in the entertainment world. But for martial music and the kind of military music, there was only one Negro band over there that topped my band. And that band was Will Vaudry's band.
Oh yeah.

The 7th Pioneer Infantry band. 807th Pioneer Infantry, Will Vaudry's. Now you see when, and Will Vaudry was such a great musician all the way around, as well as a wonderful conductor. You couldn't, there was no, there was no classification with James Reese Europe. James Reese Europe around New York gathered around himself, some important boys. And the governor favored James Reese Europe to an extent. They got most publicity out there.
Yeah, they got the most publicity out there.

And the Frenchman's loved James Europe's band for the fun they could create. But not so with Mr. Vaudry's band, the 807th. They had 57 pieces. And they were stationed down at Chamault in General J.G. Hobart's quarters down there. And that was the army headquarters for the ADF in France. But, uh, Eurus Band was never called on for that. They were called on to entertain around through war sectors.
Some people talk like Europe introduced jazz to Europe, that is James Europe's band, because they would jazz up numbers. Do you know anything about that?

I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't say that he didn't. I would say that the first acclaim the Frenchman's really give to anyone for the introduction of jazz over there came through and by the efforts of James Reese Europe. Other than, uh, than after James Reese Europe left the scene, after he was killed, I'll say that the furtherance of this was caused by Noble Sissel. And Noble Sissel carried a wonderful band over there. A wonderful band over there. Twelve pieces. I think Noble Sissel carried 18 people all together over there. Two singers and two dancers and himself, he was quite an entertainer. And his band was made up of fine musicians.
Sidney Bechet was over there about the time of the war, too.
Yeah. No, not World War I.
I thought he went over around 1918 or 1902. I don't think he was in the service.
No, he was not in the service. I think he went over with William Marion Cook's band.
That's right, yeah, he did.

And they might have introduced a sort of a modern aspect of a little ragtime with an interruption by him. But Sidney himself could not play qualifiedly in William Marion Cook's band at that time. No, he wasn't a good band.
No, no.

I know William Marion Cook personally. I knew it. Fine pianist, fine arranging, fine violinist, and a scat if you just commit one error in his music, especially in the pit. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. You see? And then there were other things about the Negro and ragtime and jazz which a few writers have disqualified, but not so. You see, the top orchestra in New York at that time was Mary Wayne and Mary Anderson and Mary Lucas because they could go to the Union and resurrect 25 pieces of hair for an occasion right out of the Union. The finest orchestra I ever heard in New York was conducted by a Negro woman, Mary Wayne. And every musician in there looked at me. They couldn't talk English because I went to the bar myself. I sneaked out of the Jacob's office band and went. And she was up there with her violin conducting. And as for band masters, I don't think no band master ever talked to Eugene Michael. I'm not saying it because he's my teacher. But you see, he personally conducted Europe's band on any intimate concert occasion where there was an official officer to arrive. You see, because Europe was a scrambling trombone player, brow beating the horn, and plunking the piano. Now, as for being an arranger of music and a musician, he was not that. But Eugene Michael was polished. You see, the man had held his seat of instructor of music. I mean the entire music department at Tuskegee. He is a graduate of Clapton University in Orangeburg, South Carolina. And one of the second teachers in the Jenkins office. That was Eugene Michael. And then he founded the Michael School of Music on Long Island in New York, Aticella. He's dead now. He has sons in New York. And if you ever go to New York to get an interview from him, find his sons and go look through that library, you'll find the Jenkins office band on his walls out there. And it's great. So contrary to some people's opinions about that, like Duke Ellington wrote in a magazine said prior to 1915 there were no Negro reading pianists. What are you going to do with him?
Yeah, that's right.
He was reading every doc you put before him, early than 1900 even. As early as 1900, as a little boy, he was schooled in his place.
He was studying music in 1900. Or he wouldn't be considered one of the best teachers down there.

Papa, I'm afraid of all of them, give him that credit. Go to Emanuel Moneta, he'll school you on the piano. He'll teach you your proper fingers. And if he wants to sit there and maybe age has got him a little bit down, but he knows all his, he's going to give you the proper execution for fingers. He can get around. See, what Duke Ellington put in his book there were no reading. What are you going to do with Tony Jackson? My God Almighty. What are you going to do with Michael, who's older than these fellas? Oh yeah. You see, Michael read every doc you put before him.
Alfred Wilson.

What are you going to do about Murray down there in Jacksonville, Florida? All those fellas who read. You see, Dr. Locke wrote a book like that too. Oh yeah, I've read that. Yeah, and I could kick him all in the pants around some place for writing that kind of thing about there were no Negro musicians, no Negro bands of consequences. He didn't know. No. So he ought to devote himself to his time to the subject he teaches in Howard and leave this part up to somebody who knows. He was a little bit of a piece of advice for Duke Ellington, he didn't come on the scene until 1927. And I happened to be in New York when he was playing with five pieces for the man whom I went to school with at Avery Normal Institute. Smalls.
Oh yeah.

And Smalls's father was one of the finest pianists organ teachers in Charleston, South Carolina. Professor Duncan, Professor Smalls, and Professor Foster, they all talked down there. And you had to read your music. So he should be ashamed to write those things unless he gets some factules about it. Who ever heard about Duke Ellington before 1900 to say any how 40? Yeah.
It was never, of course he made it all hit at the Cockney Club in 1932. That's right.

Now those things should be contradicted and should be roundly contradicted. Should be openly denounced. You want to discredit people who actually put, what are you going to do about James Rodden Johnson and Jay Rosamund Johnson who come along before any of us? Now Jay Rosamund is still alive. If he hasn't died lately. I don't think so. And a more qualified composer and an exponent of the piano you never heard in his boyhood days. His home is Jacksonville, Florida. Wendell McNeil, John McNeil, they came along ahead of Manuel's time. Oh yeah. But those fellas served as fine musicians in the Spanish-American War. And I played with Wendell. I was Wendell's trumpet player. And if Wendell didn't get me, the engagement went come from him. Because he didn't go, he didn't go look for anybody else. You had to read Wendell's scores just like that. Now Will said that he had the second Robichaux orchestra. Robichaux's main officer was in the Lyric Theater. But when Robichaux leave the orchestra, he'd come where Wendell was playing because it was his engagement. Robichaux was one of the well-known men in New Orleans, you see. So he could get these high type engagements at Antwine, at the, in the Gold Room of the Sonnyak Club. And all those places. The Roosevelt Hotel. And the, on the, what's that other big hotel there? St. Charles. St. Charles. We played in the St. Charles, too. We played in every hole there was in the St. Charles. We played in Antwine down there so many times, all them TU ducks. They used to give us half TU ducks. When Wendell's band's sitting there, your tie was speak and span. You didn't pull off a coat to play in there. Like the glue of the dance hall. The guys come in the dance hall, they just took off his coat and open up his shirt. I said, what are you going to do, fight? Well, Wendell's band's sitting there, your tie was speak and span. You had to be well-groomed. Your shoes shine. You look speak and span. And your coat buttoned as you walked through if you haven't got on your vest. And your full dress is there like anybody else. And we, a Wendell's officer, when services handed around, our service was handed right there, too, the same way. Now, that's the way New Orleans was when I was down there. And I love New Orleans. And I made no more money in New Orleans than I ever made in any place in my life. You got to cut off at you? No.
No, no, no, you're not saying anything out of the way. Oh, oh, all right.
Unless you do want to cut it off or anything. No, no, that's all right. But I'm telling you.
You're not talking about anybody except to say something good about the old music. He said a little bit about Duke, but he needs to be straight.

Yeah, he should be criticized. He should be. But as for John Robichaux's officers down there, the officers that John sent out under Wendell McNeil. Wendell was his conductor until he come on the scene. And when John come on the scene, John is king. And John take over that left-hand fiddle and start playing. And the people stop John. Hey, John, come here.
All was fine.

Wealthy people. New Orleans is loaded with a massive wealth. You know that, don't you? The Sugar Kings, the Cotton Kings, all that Dean Witter and company down there. John had to quit playing with his body on his arm, so he's walking around the floor, you see, and something once around there. But he's a celebrity like anybody else. That was John Robichaux. Mary Robinson played every duck there was on that sheet. Not a duck missing. Wendell on his violin, equally as good. And he could play some violin too. A man would tell you. He could play a French horn and he could play violin. But he was carrying the mail, you know. And he was a fine fellow, so jokish, so lovable, so sweet to talk with. Well, see, if you make a little mistake, you can't have it.
I said, but look at what we're good now. I said, are we going to play that?

All new music. They open it out in the batches right there. And you played it. Now, if he had a repertoire of that, if we played it before by request, he'd have it there. And old John was deaf on his music. Now, you wouldn't know whether John was playing his right or not, because he played left, and you could hear the things all kind of hours.
But when you could know manners.

Oh, yes. Different. But I'll say this much for them, they were great fellows. Now, all those men that were down there that established historical things in music. Somebody up here at Howard University or a Ninnicka poop around New York or a denounce it. No, no. I don't like that at all. Dr. Locke should retract every statement he uttered in his book, because none of it is true. I've told you about the band in Savannah. I've told you about the musicians down in Florida. I've told you about them in Pensacola, North of Virginia, St. Louis, all around. Well, Jenkins' band had gone and heard these musicians, so we know. We were better to give you the historical data of it than somebody like him. His foot's behind a desk in Howard University. There is where it should stay. He's delving into the face of something he doesn't know anything about. That's not the law. By the way, I think he's dead.
I'm quite sure he died a couple years or more. Anyhow, he put out a little book. Yes.
I'm pretty sure he's dead now.
Well, anyway, I read that book years ago.
I'm just trying to think about another great, yeah, Scott Joplin. Oh, yes.
My God Almighty.

What are you going to do about Blind Boone and Scott Joplin? What are you going to do about it? Now, Blind Boone did not read any music, but he had a teacher when he was a little boy. He did have his sight and he read Blind before he- He came from Missouri somewhere.
That's right. My mother always talked about him when she was a girl.

And Blind Boone played the piano so skillfully. All the compositions just as perfect. You take the school out here and look at it if you feel like it. Because he came on a concert tour to Charleston. And Professor Dart and Professor Ankrum and Professor Ranson and Professor Sawyer and Professor Smalls and Professor J. Donovan Moe, who was still alive in his 90s. Right in the same class now with Dr. Dubois. The two old men look alike. Those men were music instructors and they laid special stress on how well you played the accompaniment. Because we used to give cantatas and these dramatized versions of this thing and that thing, Martha, all of these old major compositions. I can't think of a- I can't think of a- This liturgical work on the- Vows of- The Bohemian girl-
Yeah. Yeah.

We used to give all these things in churches in Charleston. Charleston was a city noted for its finer churches. They had a corner meeting house like they have today. You see Charleston had about 11 churches in it. All cathedral styles. Plush floors. Fine seats. Centenary church. Emanuel. Big Emanuel and Little Emanuel. But they were both magnitudes and size. A house. Thousands and more people. Balkans all around. Pipe organ. The biggest pipe she ever laid out on. And they chimed. And you can hear the chimes in Charleston until today. And the Negro churches had pipe organs just equal to any of them. You could go to any of them. Those are fine churches. Now all these men. They sat as conductors or organists in these trials. And the services were just fine. They didn't have this raucous type of service. These things like Church of God Christ and stomping all around here. They came on the scene here in the last 25 years. You see. And all these men I mentioned to you had- They were choir masters. Organists and conductors with choir in these various churches. See. Asked Edmund. And Edmund was an old man in New York. Asked him about his father. I'm going to ask you a bit more about Scott Joplin if you knew him.
Knew him personally. Knew him personally. Knew him personally.

He came to the band in Atlantic City while we were engaged on the boardwalk there. Young's Million Dollar Pear in Atlantic City was where the Jenkins band was playing. When Scott Joplin walked out and brought his rag. The Maple Leaf Rag. Right. Then he brought- The first I ever heard of the Bolo Rag. Sweet Meats. And then I don't know whether he wrote Temptation or not but those four were the featured rags with the band.
Well now when I went to New Orleans I started putting that double beat on it like that.

We used to play it like a ragtime should be played. You see. Ought to be played those days. Of course the boys in New Orleans put a different touch on it. Scott Joplin presented Alonzo Hardy with the Maple Leaf Rag and these other three rags there and told him, well you can have these if you're playing for me. And Alonzo issued the parts out and said, well, we'll have to play it for you. Because there wasn't anything too tough for Alonzo Hardy. He was the first bandmaster I had been in the college. John Brown succeeded him. I succeeded John Brown. Of course they expelled me. Dr. Osmond told me the college could never do without you the next year. But Alonzo Hardy was our bandmaster and a great bandmaster. See he became bandmaster in the 15th Regiment of New York in his latter years. And he died in New York. They told me, so they told me that he drank everything. I wouldn't doubt it.

Well anyway, you've certainly explained a lot of things and directed a lot of false notions about music. I hope I have. I hope I have. Your broad experience is invaluable in being all over the country, which a lot of people have never had. That's right. Travel from one end of the country to the other and play and see everybody. Music all over the country. Thank you. It gives you a wonderful broad view of it.

Yeah. As near as I can give it to you, those are true happenings throughout my entire life. My encounter with the, or however these things would never have happened to me were, I committed to becoming an inmate of the Jenkins Orphanies. I have to credit the Jenkins Orphanies for the major happenings in my life. It was on account of me being an orphan, being admitted to the Jenkins Orphanies, being taken in there by the founder, that I enjoyed these privileges. Of course, the training I got in the Jenkins Orphanies furthered the success of these things. From the training they gave me, it allowed me to travel more extensively. Otherwise, I'd never been, if I had never studied the cornet or any music of any type, why, I'd never been found with any shows. Of course, my mother wanted me to be a preacher, and later years, some of the folks around wanted me to be a doctor, and for my part, I wanted to be a lawyer. And so then I discovered that there wasn't much for a lawyer to do. I didn't think he had much success. And yet, while I was in the Army, I took the law course over there, because you would allow me to apply for most any course you wanted. Have you seen one of my letterheads?
I'll turn this off. Oh, okay. Thank you very much.
Thank you.

segments.title: Birth, parents and siblings in South Carolina
segments.summary: White gives his birth date, parents, siblings, and his mother's work as a rural schoolteacher before he was placed in the Jenkins orphanage.

segments.title: The Jenkins orphanage, Reverend Jenkins and White's baptism
segments.summary: White describes the founding of the orphanage, Reverend Jenkins and his churches, and being baptized at fourteen.

segments.title: Learning music: printing shop, alto horn and the band's first Eastern tour
segments.summary: With no musical family, White worked in the printing department until about fourteen, then joined the orphanage band on alto horn under Eugene Michael.

segments.title: Eastern tours and the Atlantic City boardwalk engagement
segments.summary: The band played concerts across the East, including a month beside Arthur Pryor's band in Atlantic City; White notes its earlier fame at fairs and in London.

segments.title: Size of the Jenkins band, inaugural parades and bands White heard around the country
segments.summary: White describes band strength, the inaugural parades of 1904, 1908 and 1912, Edmund Jenkins, and the Black bands he met in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and elsewhere.

segments.title: Leaving Benedict College after drinking with Pinckney's band
segments.summary: White names the band's directors, then tells how Benedict's president told him to leave because he took a drink while playing with Tom Pinckney's band.

segments.title: Marriage, Jacksonville concert band and the Uncle Tom's Cabin job in New York
segments.summary: After marrying the president's daughter White worked as a printer and led the Jacksonville Concert Band until Mr. Jenkins called him back to take a unit to New York.

segments.title: Franks Minstrels and the Alabama Minstrels under Jeff Smith
segments.summary: White began touring with minstrel shows, joining Jeff Smith's Alabama Minstrels and praising Smith as a cornet soloist.

segments.title: Taking over the minstrel band and meeting the Verrett brothers in Homer, Louisiana
segments.summary: White describes the minstrel orchestra, becoming bandmaster, and playing a winter in Homer with the Verrett brothers' seven-piece band.

segments.title: New Orleans style compared with the playing in Jacksonville and elsewhere
segments.summary: White says the Louisiana style, with its beat and variations, was unlike anything elsewhere, whereas Jacksonville musicians stuck to the note.

segments.title: Interruption by a phone call
segments.summary: The talk pauses for a telephone call and a brief exchange.

segments.title: Cole Brothers Circus and the minstrel units under J.C. Miles
segments.summary: White describes the 1918 season with the Cole Brothers Circus, its owners, and the bands of the Virginia, Alabama and Georgia minstrel shows.
